dropped.reason: Year 11 content (not examined in the HSC): molar enthalpy of combustion of glucose and reaction stoichiometry (Modules 2 and 4)

questions.question: How many structural isomers have the formula $\text{C}_3\text{H}_6\text{BrCl}$?
questions.answer: The Br and Cl are attached to a 3-carbon chain. Both on the same carbon: 1-bromo-1-chloropropane and 2-bromo-2-chloropropane. On adjacent carbons: 1-bromo-2-chloropropane and 2-bromo-1-chloropropane. On the two end carbons: 1-bromo-3-chloropropane. That gives 5 isomers in total.

questions.question: The diagram shows the components of an atomic absorption spectrophotometer. Which component is changed when testing a range of different elements?
questions.answer: AAS uses a hollow cathode lamp made of the element being analysed. It emits the exact wavelengths that atoms of that element absorb. So a different lamp is needed for each element. The flame, monochromator and detector stay the same.

questions.question: Which of the following has the best atom economy in the production of an organic molecule?
questions.answer: Adding $\text{Br}_2$ to propene is an addition reaction: $\text{CH}_2{=}\text{CHCH}_3 + \text{Br}_2 \rightarrow \text{CH}_2\text{BrCHBrCH}_3$. All reactant atoms end up in the one product, so the atom economy is 100%. The substitution reactions also make by-products ($\text{HI}$ and $\text{NaCl}$). Combustion produces no organic molecule at all.

questions.question: Which option below names TWO functional groups in this molecule?
questions.answer: The molecule is $\text{H}_2\text{N–CH}_2\text{–CH}_2\text{–CH(OH)–CH}_2\text{CH}_3$. The $-\text{NH}_2$ group is an amine and the $-\text{OH}$ group is a hydroxyl. There is no $\text{C}{=}\text{O}$, so it has no amide. An ethyl group is an alkyl substituent, not a functional group.

questions.question: A chemist conducted a flame test experiment to determine the species of metal ion present in a solution from an unlabelled bottle. Upon testing, they witnessed a flame with a blue/grey colour. Which of the following metal cations was responsible for this observation?
questions.answer: Lead(II) gives a pale blue/grey-white flame. Calcium gives brick red. Magnesium gives no characteristic colour, and iron does not give a blue/grey flame.

questions.question: One traditional way in which cycad fruit has been made safe to consume is by placing the cut seeds in a basket and placing them in a stream for several days. Which concept is demonstrated by this process?
questions.answer: Running water keeps carrying away the dissolved toxin, so matter leaves the system: it is an open system. Because the toxin never builds up in the surrounding water, equilibrium is never reached. More toxin keeps dissolving out of the seeds until almost all of it has been removed.

questions.question: The infrared spectrum has been provided for an unknown organic compound. What functional group is present in this compound?
questions.answer: There are two N–H absorptions near 3350 and 3180 cm$^{-1}$ (an $-\text{NH}_2$ group) and a very strong C=O absorption near 1650 cm$^{-1}$. Together these indicate an amide. An amine has no C=O peak. A carboxylic acid would show a very broad O–H band from 2500 to 3300 cm$^{-1}$ and a C=O near 1710 cm$^{-1}$. An ester would show C=O near 1740 cm$^{-1}$ and no N–H peaks.

questions.question: Consider the molecular structure below: $$\text{CH}_3\text{–CH}_2\text{–COO–CH}_2\text{–CH}_3$$ Which of the following identifies the compound and the substances that could be used to synthesise it?
options: propyl ethanoate: propan-1-ol and ethanoic acid
propyl ethanoate: ethanol and propanoic acid
ethyl propanoate: ethanoic acid and propan-1-ol
ethyl propanoate: propanoic acid and ethanol
questions.answer: The acid part $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{COO}-$ (3 C, including the C=O carbon) is propanoate. The alkyl group on the O, $-\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$, is ethyl. So the ester is ethyl propanoate, made from propanoic acid and ethanol.

questions.question: The table provides information about three organic compounds X, Y and Z, each with molar mass 60 g mol$^{-1}$. The boiling point of X (propan-1-ol) is 97 °C and of Y (ethanoic acid) is 118 °C. Which of the following is the best estimate for the boiling point of compound Z?
questions.answer: Z is methyl methanoate, an ester. It has no O–H group, so its molecules cannot hydrogen bond to each other. Only dipole–dipole and dispersion forces act between them. Its boiling point is therefore far below those of X and Y, which have the same molar mass but can hydrogen bond. The only reasonable choice is 32 °C.

questions.question: Interactions between soap anions and water solvent molecules can result in the formation of micelles as shown in the diagram. Which alternative below correctly describes the interactions in the micelle?
options: The polar alkyl tails line up inside the micelle experiencing dispersion forces and the non-polar carboxylate heads on the outside of the micelle form ion-dipole interactions with the water solvent.

The polar alkyl tails line up inside the micelle experiencing ion-dipole interactions and the non-polar carboxylate heads on the outside of the micelle experience dispersion forces with the water solvent.
The non-polar alkyl tails line up inside the micelle experiencing dispersion forces and the polar carboxylate heads on the outside of the micelle form ion-dipole interactions with the water solvent.
The non-polar alkyl tails line up inside the micelle forming ion-dipole interactions and the polar carboxylate heads on the outside of the micelle experience dispersion forces with the water solvent.
questions.answer: The hydrocarbon tails are non-polar. They cluster in the centre of the micelle, held by dispersion forces. The charged $-\text{COO}^-$ heads face outward and form ion–dipole attractions with the water molecules.

questions.question: Ethanol can be prepared by the fermentation of glucose. What volume of carbon dioxide gas is produced when 9.00 g of glucose completely ferments at 298 K and 100 kPa? (Molar volume of a gas at 298 K and 100 kPa = 24.79 L mol$^{-1}$.)
questions.answer:
$\text{C}_6\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_6 \rightarrow 2\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{OH} + 2\text{CO}_2$

$n(\text{glucose}) = \dfrac{9.00}{180.16} = 0.04996$ mol, so $n(\text{CO}_2) = 2 \times 0.04996 = 0.09992$ mol.

$V = 0.09992 \times 24.79 = 2.48$ L

questions.question: The skeletal formula for an organic compound is given. Which of the following shows the correct splitting pattern in the proton NMR spectrum for the indicated environment?
questions.answer: The compound is 3-methylpentanoic acid. The arrow points to the $\text{CH}_2$ of the ethyl branch. Its neighbouring carbons carry 1 H (the CH) and 3 H (the $\text{CH}_3$), giving 4 neighbouring hydrogens. By the $n+1$ rule the signal splits into 5 peaks, a quintet, which is pattern D. (A is a doublet, B a triplet and C a quartet.)

questions.question: Consider the section of a polyester shown. Which of the following is a monomer of this polymer?
questions.answer: The repeating unit is $-\text{O–CH(CH}_3\text{)–CO}-$, so each monomer has 3 carbons with a $\text{CH}_3$ group on the carbon that carries the oxygen. The monomer is 2-hydroxypropanoic acid (lactic acid), $\text{CH}_3\text{CH(OH)COOH}$. Its $-\text{OH}$ and $-\text{COOH}$ groups condense to form the ester links of poly(lactic acid).

questions.question: Consider the structural formula of the molecule presented. How many unique signals would be presented in the $^{13}$C NMR spectrum?
questions.answer: The central quaternary carbon carries three equivalent ethyl groups and one $-\text{CH}_2\text{OCH}_3$ group. The carbon environments are: the 3 equivalent $\text{CH}_3$ of the ethyls, the 3 equivalent $\text{CH}_2$ of the ethyls, the quaternary C, the $\text{CH}_2\text{–O}$, and the $\text{O–CH}_3$. That is 5 signals.

questions.question: A pair of unlabelled beakers contains separate solutions of lead and barium ions. Which of the following methods could be used to confirm the presence of both ions?
options: Performing a flame test and recording the colours observed.
Adding potassium hydroxide and comparing the precipitate colours.
Adding sodium sulfate and comparing the precipitate colours.
Adding magnesium chloride and comparing the precipitate colours.
questions.answer:
With hydroxide, $\text{Pb}^{2+}$ forms a white precipitate of $\text{Pb(OH)}_2$, but $\text{Ba(OH)}_2$ is soluble and no precipitate forms with $\text{Ba}^{2+}$. So the two beakers behave differently. Sodium sulfate gives white precipitates ($\text{PbSO}_4$ and $\text{BaSO}_4$) with both ions, so it cannot tell them apart.

*Note: the paper's key accepts both B and D. With chloride, only $\text{Pb}^{2+}$ forms a precipitate ($\text{PbCl}_2$), although $\text{PbCl}_2$ is fairly soluble and only precipitates from concentrated solutions.*

questions.question: How many moles of magnesium hydroxide will dissolve in 1.0 L of water? ($K_{sp}$ of $\text{Mg(OH)}_2 = 5.61 \times 10^{-12}$ at 25 °C.)
questions.answer:
$\text{Mg(OH)}_2(s) \rightleftharpoons \text{Mg}^{2+}(aq) + 2\text{OH}^-(aq)$. If $s$ mol L$^{-1}$ dissolves, then $K_{sp} = s(2s)^2 = 4s^3$.
$$s = \sqrt[3]{\frac{5.61 \times 10^{-12}}{4}} = 1.12 \times 10^{-4}\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$$
So about $1 \times 10^{-4}$ mol dissolves in 1.0 L.

questions.question: An equal volume of hydrochloric acid solution and a citric acid solution were found to have the same pH. The structure of citric acid is given. Which statement is correct concerning the citric acid solution?
options: Both solutions contain the same number of intact acid molecules.
Both solutions contain the same number of ions.
The hydrochloric acid solution has a higher concentration of hydrogen ions.
The citric acid has a higher concentration of intact acid molecules than hydrochloric acid.
questions.answer: Equal pH means equal $[\text{H}^+]$, so C is wrong. HCl is a strong acid and is essentially fully ionised, leaving no intact HCl molecules. Citric acid is a weak acid and only a small fraction of its molecules ionise. To give the same $[\text{H}^+]$, the citric acid solution must be much more concentrated, and most of its molecules remain un-ionised.

questions.question: A student diluted a solution of a strong acid by mixing 25 mL of acid with 75 mL of water. If the original acid solution had a pH of 3.1, what is the final pH of the acid solution after dilution?
questions.answer:
$[\text{H}^+] = 10^{-3.1} = 7.94 \times 10^{-4}$ mol L$^{-1}$. The volume goes from 25 mL to 100 mL (a factor of 4), so the new $[\text{H}^+] = 1.99 \times 10^{-4}$ mol L$^{-1}$.
$$\text{pH} = -\log_{10}(1.99 \times 10^{-4}) = 3.7$$

questions.question:
Which molecule is consistent with the series of observations provided?

| Source | Information |
|---|---|
| Chemical test | Reacts with sodium carbonate powder to produce gas. |
| Infrared spectrum | 3 key signals: broad signal at 3480 cm$^{-1}$; strong signal at 3150 cm$^{-1}$; strong signal at 1720 cm$^{-1}$ |
| Proton NMR | 4 unique signals: 1 H singlet; 2 H doublet; 1 H multiplet; 3 H doublet |
questions.answer:
Producing gas ($\text{CO}_2$) with sodium carbonate, a broad O–H band and C=O at 1720 cm$^{-1}$ all point to a carboxylic acid, which rules out C (aldehyde) and D (ketone). Pentanoic acid (B) has 5 proton environments with no doublets. 3-Methylbutanoic acid (A), $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{CHCH}_2\text{COOH}$, has 4 environments:
- COOH: 1 H singlet
- $\text{CH}_2$: doublet
- CH: multiplet
- $\text{CH}_3$ groups: doublet

*Note: the two methyl groups are equivalent, so that doublet is really 6 H, not the 3 H stated in the table. A is still the only consistent option.*

questions.question: Butanoic acid, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{COOH}$, is shown below. Draw different isomers of butanoic acid: (i) a chain isomer, (ii) a functional group isomer.
questions.answer:
**Chain isomer:** 2-methylpropanoic acid, $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{CHCOOH}$. It has the same carboxylic acid group, but the carbon chain is branched.

**Functional group isomer:** an ester with formula $\text{C}_4\text{H}_8\text{O}_2$, for example methyl propanoate, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{COOCH}_3$. Ethyl ethanoate, $\text{CH}_3\text{COOCH}_2\text{CH}_3$, and propyl methanoate, $\text{HCOOCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$, are also correct.

questions.question: The rates of the forward and reverse reactions for a closed system are shown on the graph. Sketch on a copy of the graph how the rates of reaction change when the same initial concentrations are used in the same reaction vessel in the presence of a catalyst.
questions.answer: A catalyst gives an alternative pathway with lower activation energy for both the forward and reverse reactions. So both rates are higher at every point. The new forward curve starts higher and falls more steeply, and the new reverse curve rises more steeply. The two curves meet sooner, so equilibrium is reached in less time. At equilibrium the forward and reverse rates are again equal, but at a higher rate than without the catalyst. The equilibrium position itself does not change (dashed curves below).

questions.question: Describe a chemical test that could be used to identify the functional group present in the following molecule (butan-2-ol) and provide a relevant observation to confirm its presence.
questions.answer:
The molecule contains a hydroxyl group (it is a secondary alcohol). Add a few drops of acidified potassium permanganate solution ($\text{H}^+/\text{MnO}_4^-$) and warm gently. The secondary alcohol is oxidised to a ketone (butan-2-one), and the purple permanganate is decolourised. This confirms the alcohol functional group.

Other acceptable tests:
- Adding a small piece of sodium metal produces bubbles of hydrogen gas.
- Lucas reagent (zinc chloride in concentrated HCl) turns the solution cloudy after a few minutes for a secondary alcohol.

questions.question:
A 0.2845 g sample of impure sodium carbonate required 22.65 mL of a hydrochloric acid solution for titration. A 0.2204 g sample of pure calcium carbonate required 20.06 mL of the hydrochloric acid solution of the same concentration.

Write a balanced chemical equation for the sodium carbonate reaction.
questions.answer: $$\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3(s) + 2\text{HCl}(aq) \rightarrow 2\text{NaCl}(aq) + \text{CO}_2(g) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(l)$$

questions.question:
A 0.2845 g sample of impure sodium carbonate required 22.65 mL of a hydrochloric acid solution for titration. A 0.2204 g sample of pure calcium carbonate required 20.06 mL of the hydrochloric acid solution of the same concentration.

What is the percentage of sodium carbonate in the sample?
questions.answer:
**Standardise the HCl using $\text{CaCO}_3$:** $\text{CaCO}_3 + 2\text{HCl} \rightarrow \text{CaCl}_2 + \text{CO}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O}$

$n(\text{CaCO}_3) = \dfrac{0.2204}{100.09} = 2.202 \times 10^{-3}$ mol, so $n(\text{HCl}) = 2 \times 2.202 \times 10^{-3} = 4.404 \times 10^{-3}$ mol.

$c(\text{HCl}) = \dfrac{4.404 \times 10^{-3}}{0.02006} = 0.2195$ mol L$^{-1}$

**Analyse the sodium carbonate sample:**

$n(\text{HCl}) = 0.2195 \times 0.02265 = 4.973 \times 10^{-3}$ mol

$n(\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3) = \tfrac{1}{2} \times 4.973 \times 10^{-3} = 2.486 \times 10^{-3}$ mol

$m(\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3) = 2.486 \times 10^{-3} \times 105.99 = 0.2635$ g

$$\%\ \text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3 = \frac{0.2635}{0.2845} \times 100 = 92.6\%$$

questions.question: Justify the use of sodium hydrogen carbonate in cleaning up acid spills in the laboratory.
questions.answer:
Sodium hydrogen carbonate is amphiprotic and acts as a weak base (proton acceptor). It neutralises the acid: $\text{HCO}_3^-(aq) + \text{H}^+(aq) \rightarrow \text{H}_2\text{O}(l) + \text{CO}_2(g)$.

Because it is only a weak base, any excess added is not corrosive or hazardous, so it can be used generously. The fizzing of $\text{CO}_2$ gives a visual sign: when the bubbling stops, neutralisation is complete. As a cheap solid powder it can also be sprinkled around and onto the spill to contain it.

questions.question: Sodium hydrogen carbonate, $\text{NaHCO}_3$, is used to clean up acid spills. In Arrhenius' laboratory in 1884, would he have advised the use of this same substance to clean the acid spill? Give TWO reasons for your answer.
questions.answer:
No, Arrhenius would not have advised using sodium hydrogen carbonate.
1. In Arrhenius' theory a base is a substance that dissociates in water to produce hydroxide ions, $\text{OH}^-$. $\text{NaHCO}_3$ contains no hydroxide, so he would not have classified it as a base able to neutralise the acid.
2. His theory applies only to substances dissolved in water. Solid $\text{NaHCO}_3$ reacts directly with the acid spill, and its amphiprotic behaviour (accepting a proton from the acid) is only explained by the later Brønsted–Lowry theory.

questions.question:
The Haber process is still used for the industrial production of ammonia:
$$3\text{H}_2(g) + \text{N}_2(g) \rightleftharpoons 2\text{NH}_3(g) \qquad \Delta H = -92.4\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$$
In a conventional chemical plant, an efficient process is achieved through the use of an iron catalyst with high pressure and low temperature conditions. An outline of the chemical process in this plant is given in the diagram.

With reference to the diagram, identify THREE design features, other than those outlined above, and explain the economic benefits they provide.
questions.answer:
1. **Recycling of unreacted gases.** Only a fraction of the $\text{N}_2$ and $\text{H}_2$ is converted to ammonia in each pass through the catalytic chamber. The unreacted gases are returned to the compressor and passed over the catalyst again. This raises the overall conversion of reactants close to 100% and greatly reduces raw material costs.
2. **Heat exchanger.** The forward reaction is exothermic, so the gas leaving the catalytic chamber is hot. The heat exchanger transfers this heat to the incoming cold reactant gases, preheating them to the operating temperature. This reduces the energy (fuel) costs of running the plant.
3. **Condenser at −20 °C.** Ammonia has a much higher boiling point than $\text{N}_2$ and $\text{H}_2$ because of hydrogen bonding, so cooling liquefies only the ammonia. This is a cheap, simple way to separate the product from the unreacted gases. The liquid ammonia is also compact and economical to store and transport. Removing the product also allows the unreacted gases to be recycled.

Other valid features: the raw materials come from cheap, abundant sources ($\text{N}_2$ from the fractional distillation of air, $\text{H}_2$ as a by-product of cracking crude oil), which lowers material costs.

questions.question:
The biofuel 2-methylpropan-1-ol ($\text{C}_4\text{H}_9\text{OH}$, $M = 74.12$ g mol$^{-1}$) can be produced from proteins. 2-Methylpropan-1-ol can be used in petrol engines and has a heat of combustion of 36.1 kJ g$^{-1}$ at 298 K.

Account for the difference between the heat of combustion of octane (5470 kJ mol$^{-1}$) and 2-methylpropan-1-ol.
questions.answer:
Convert to the same units:
- Octane: $\dfrac{5470}{114.23} = 47.9$ kJ g$^{-1}$
- 2-Methylpropan-1-ol: $36.1 \times 74.12 = 2676$ kJ mol$^{-1}$

So octane releases about twice as much energy per mole and about 33% more per gram.

**Per mole:** octane ($\text{C}_8\text{H}_{18}$) has more carbon and hydrogen atoms per molecule than $\text{C}_4\text{H}_9\text{OH}$:
$$\text{C}_8\text{H}_{18} + \tfrac{25}{2}\text{O}_2 \rightarrow 8\text{CO}_2 + 9\text{H}_2\text{O}$$
$$\text{C}_4\text{H}_9\text{OH} + 6\text{O}_2 \rightarrow 4\text{CO}_2 + 5\text{H}_2\text{O}$$
Burning octane forms many more C=O and O–H bonds (17 mol of products versus 9). Bond formation releases energy, so more energy is released overall.

**Per gram:** the alcohol already contains an oxygen atom and is partly oxidised. This oxygen adds mass but releases no energy on combustion, so the alcohol releases less energy per gram than the hydrocarbon.

questions.question:
The biofuel 2-methylpropan-1-ol ($\text{C}_4\text{H}_9\text{OH}$, $M = 74.12$ g mol$^{-1}$) can be produced from proteins. 2-Methylpropan-1-ol can be used in petrol engines and has a heat of combustion of 36.1 kJ g$^{-1}$ at 298 K.

A small fuel burner containing 2.36 g of 2-methylpropan-1-ol was placed directly under a beaker containing 500.0 g of water at standard laboratory conditions. Calculate the maximum temperature that the water could reach if the contents of the fuel burner underwent complete combustion. The initial temperature of the water was 298 K. (Specific heat capacity of water = 4.18 J g$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$.)
questions.answer:
Energy released: $q = 36.1\ \text{kJ g}^{-1} \times 2.36\ \text{g} = 85.2$ kJ $= 8.52 \times 10^4$ J

(Equivalently: $n = \dfrac{2.36}{74.12} = 0.03184$ mol, and $0.03184 \times 2676 = 85.2$ kJ.)

Assuming all of this heat is absorbed by the water, $q = mc\Delta T$:
$$\Delta T = \frac{8.52 \times 10^4}{500.0 \times 4.18} = 40.8\ \text{K}$$
Maximum temperature $= 298 + 40.8 = 339$ K (about 65.8 °C).

questions.question:
The solubility of a series of alcohols at 298 K is given in the table.

| Alcohol | Solubility in water (g L$^{-1}$) |
|---|---|
| Butan-1-ol | 73 |
| Pentan-1-ol | 22 |
| Heptan-1-ol | 2.0 |
| Octan-1-ol | 0.5 |

Plot the solubility against the number of carbon atoms in the alcohols (number of carbons from 4 to 8 on the horizontal axis).
questions.answer: Plot the number of carbon atoms (4–8) on the horizontal axis and solubility (g L$^{-1}$, from 0 to 80) on the vertical axis, with a labelled axis and a suitable scale. Plot the four points (4, 73), (5, 22), (7, 2.0) and (8, 0.5). Draw a smooth curve of best fit through them. Solubility falls steeply at first and then levels off towards zero.

questions.question:
The solubility of a series of alcohols at 298 K is given in the table.

| Alcohol | Solubility in water (g L$^{-1}$) |
|---|---|
| Butan-1-ol | 73 |
| Pentan-1-ol | 22 |
| Heptan-1-ol | 2.0 |
| Octan-1-ol | 0.5 |

Using a graph of these data, estimate the solubility of hexan-1-ol in g L$^{-1}$.
questions.answer: Read the curve of best fit at 6 carbon atoms: the solubility of hexan-1-ol is about 9 g L$^{-1}$ (any value of about 7–10 g L$^{-1}$ read correctly from the curve). The accepted value is about 6 g L$^{-1}$.

questions.question:
The solubility of a series of alcohols at 298 K is given in the table.

| Alcohol | Solubility in water (g L$^{-1}$) |
|---|---|
| Butan-1-ol | 73 |
| Pentan-1-ol | 22 |
| Heptan-1-ol | 2.0 |
| Octan-1-ol | 0.5 |

Use the data to explain the trend in the solubilities of these alcohols. Draw a relevant diagram to support your answer.
questions.answer:
Solubility in water decreases sharply as the carbon chain gets longer, from 73 g L$^{-1}$ for butan-1-ol to only 0.5 g L$^{-1}$ for octan-1-ol.

Each alcohol has one polar hydroxyl group. Its $\text{O}^{\delta-}$ and $\text{H}^{\delta+}$ can form hydrogen bonds with water molecules (solute–solvent attractions), as shown in the diagram, and this is what lets the alcohol dissolve. The rest of the molecule is a non-polar hydrocarbon chain. It cannot hydrogen bond to water and only forms weak dispersion forces with it. It also disrupts the hydrogen-bonded network between water molecules.

As the chain lengthens, the non-polar part becomes a larger fraction of the molecule, and the single –OH group has less influence. The dispersion forces between the long alcohol chains themselves (solute–solute attractions) also become stronger. These attractions are not replaced by equally strong attractions to water, so the longer-chain alcohols become less soluble in polar water.

questions.question:
The water gas shift reaction can be used to produce hydrogen gas and consume toxic carbon monoxide:
$$\text{CO}(g) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(g) \rightleftharpoons \text{CO}_2(g) + \text{H}_2(g)$$
The equilibrium constant for this reaction is highly temperature sensitive, as shown in the graph.

Justify whether this reaction is exothermic or endothermic.
questions.answer:
$$K_{eq} = \frac{[\text{CO}_2][\text{H}_2]}{[\text{CO}][\text{H}_2\text{O}]}$$
The graph shows that $K_{eq}$ decreases as the temperature increases: it falls from about 138 at 500 K to almost 1 at 1000 K. A smaller $K_{eq}$ means that at higher temperatures the equilibrium mixture contains less product and more reactant, so the equilibrium has shifted to the left.

By Le Chatelier's principle, raising the temperature favours the endothermic direction, which absorbs the added heat. Since raising the temperature favours the reverse reaction, the reverse reaction is endothermic. Therefore the forward reaction is exothermic ($\Delta H < 0$).

In terms of rates: heating increases the rate of the reverse reaction more than the forward reaction. So the reverse reaction has the larger activation energy, which is again consistent with an exothermic forward reaction.

questions.question:
The water gas shift reaction can be used to produce hydrogen gas and consume toxic carbon monoxide:
$$\text{CO}(g) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(g) \rightleftharpoons \text{CO}_2(g) + \text{H}_2(g)$$
The equilibrium constant for this reaction is highly temperature sensitive, as shown in the graph.

$6.7 \times 10^{-3}$ mol of CO, 4.5 mol of $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ and 0.4 mol of $\text{CO}_2$ were placed into a 5.0 L sealed reaction vessel at 500 K. Using the graph ($K_{eq} \approx 138$ at 500 K), calculate the concentration of $\text{H}_2$ at equilibrium.
questions.answer:
Initial concentrations ($n/5.0$): $[\text{CO}] = 1.34 \times 10^{-3}$, $[\text{H}_2\text{O}] = 0.90$, $[\text{CO}_2] = 0.080$, $[\text{H}_2] = 0$ mol L$^{-1}$.

| | CO | $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ | $\text{CO}_2$ | $\text{H}_2$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| I | $1.34 \times 10^{-3}$ | 0.90 | 0.080 | 0 |
| C | $-x$ | $-x$ | $+x$ | $+x$ |
| E | $1.34 \times 10^{-3} - x$ | $0.90 - x$ | $0.080 + x$ | $x$ |

$$138 = \frac{(0.080 + x)\,x}{(1.34 \times 10^{-3} - x)(0.90 - x)}$$
Since $x \le 1.34 \times 10^{-3}$, it is negligible compared with 0.080 and 0.90:
$$138 \approx \frac{0.080\,x}{(1.34 \times 10^{-3} - x)(0.90)}$$
$$1552.5\,(1.34 \times 10^{-3} - x) = x \quad\Rightarrow\quad x = \frac{2.080}{1553.5} = 1.339 \times 10^{-3}$$
Solving the full quadratic gives the same value. Almost all of the CO reacts because $K$ is large and water is in large excess.
$$[\text{H}_2] = 1.34 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$$

questions.question:
A beaker containing pieces of copper and silver, along with a solution of their ions, is at equilibrium at $t = 0$:
$$\text{Cu}(s) + 2\text{Ag}^+(aq) \rightleftharpoons 2\text{Ag}(s) + \text{Cu}^{2+}(aq)$$

Identify the effect on the equilibrium position of adding another piece of copper metal to the beaker.
questions.answer: There is no change to the equilibrium position. Copper is a pure solid, so its concentration is constant and it does not appear in the equilibrium expression $K = \dfrac{[\text{Cu}^{2+}]}{[\text{Ag}^+]^2}$. Adding more solid does not change $Q$.

questions.question:
A beaker containing pieces of copper and silver, along with a solution of their ions, is at equilibrium at $t = 0$:
$$\text{Cu}(s) + 2\text{Ag}^+(aq) \rightleftharpoons 2\text{Ag}(s) + \text{Cu}^{2+}(aq)$$

Water is added to double the volume of the solution at $t = 1$, immediately reducing the intensity of the blue colour. The system then re-establishes equilibrium at $t = 2$. Account for changes in appearance of the beaker contents between $t = 1$ and $t = 2$.
questions.answer:
At equilibrium $Q = K = \dfrac{[\text{Cu}^{2+}]}{[\text{Ag}^+]^2}$. Doubling the volume halves both concentrations:
$$Q = \frac{\tfrac12[\text{Cu}^{2+}]}{\left(\tfrac12[\text{Ag}^+]\right)^2} = 2K$$
Since $Q > K$, the system shifts to the left (the reverse reaction is favoured) until $Q = K$ again. Le Chatelier's principle agrees: dilution lowers the total concentration of dissolved ions, so the system favours the side with more aqueous ions (2 $\text{Ag}^+$ versus 1 $\text{Cu}^{2+}$).

Between $t = 1$ and $t = 2$, silver metal is oxidised to $\text{Ag}^+$ and blue $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ ions are reduced to copper. As a result:
- the solution becomes an even paler blue as $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ is consumed;
- the amount of silver metal decreases;
- more reddish-brown copper metal appears in the beaker.

questions.question: 2.53 g of KSCN was dissolved in a 250.0 mL volumetric flask. It was added to 125 mL of 0.108 mol L$^{-1}$ lead(II) acetate. 2.19 g of lead thiocyanate precipitate was formed. Calculate the value of the $K_{sp}$ for lead thiocyanate.
questions.answer:
$$\text{Pb}^{2+}(aq) + 2\text{SCN}^-(aq) \rightleftharpoons \text{Pb(SCN)}_2(s)$$
**Moles before and after precipitation:**

| Quantity | Calculation | Moles |
|---|---|---|
| $\text{Pb(SCN)}_2$ precipitated | $\dfrac{2.19}{323.38}$ | $6.772 \times 10^{-3}$ |
| KSCN added | $\dfrac{2.53}{97.19}$ | $2.603 \times 10^{-2}$ |
| $\text{Pb}^{2+}$ added | $0.108 \times 0.125$ | $1.350 \times 10^{-2}$ |
| $\text{Pb}^{2+}$ left in solution | $0.01350 - 0.006772$ | $6.728 \times 10^{-3}$ |
| $\text{SCN}^-$ left in solution | $0.02603 - 2(0.006772)$ | $1.249 \times 10^{-2}$ |

**Concentrations** (total volume $= 0.2500 + 0.125 = 0.375$ L):
- $[\text{Pb}^{2+}] = \dfrac{6.728 \times 10^{-3}}{0.375} = 1.794 \times 10^{-2}$ mol L$^{-1}$
- $[\text{SCN}^-] = \dfrac{1.249 \times 10^{-2}}{0.375} = 3.330 \times 10^{-2}$ mol L$^{-1}$

**$K_{sp}$:**
$$K_{sp} = [\text{Pb}^{2+}][\text{SCN}^-]^2 = (1.794 \times 10^{-2})(3.330 \times 10^{-2})^2 = 1.99 \times 10^{-5}$$

questions.question: The reaction pathway shown begins with hex-3-ene. Hex-3-ene reacts with HBr(aq) to give compound J, and is converted to hexan-3-ol. Hexan-3-ol reacts with acidified permanganate ($\text{H}^+/\text{MnO}_4^-$) to give compound K, and with compound M in the presence of $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4(l)$ to give compound L (structure shown). Justify the identification of compounds J, M and K.
questions.answer:
**J is 3-bromohexane**, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CHBrCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$. HBr adds across the C=C double bond of hex-3-ene (an addition reaction). The H bonds to one carbon of the double bond and the Br to the other. Hex-3-ene is symmetrical, so only one product forms.

**M is ethanoic acid**, $\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$. Compound L is the ester hexan-3-yl ethanoate, $\text{CH}_3\text{COOCH(CH}_2\text{CH}_3)\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$. An ester forms when an alcohol reacts with a carboxylic acid, with concentrated sulfuric acid as a catalyst (esterification). The alkyl part of L comes from hexan-3-ol. The acid part, $\text{CH}_3\text{COO}-$, has two carbons, so the acid added must be ethanoic acid.

**K is hexan-3-one**, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{COCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$. Hexan-3-ol is a secondary alcohol, because its –OH carbon is bonded to two other carbons. Acidified permanganate oxidises secondary alcohols to ketones (the purple colour fades), and the ketone is not oxidised further.

questions.question: Draw an equation, using structural formulae, for the conversion of hex-3-ene to hexan-3-ol, indicating the reagent(s) required.
questions.answer:
Hydration of the alkene: water adds across the double bond, with dilute sulfuric acid (or phosphoric acid) as a catalyst and heat.
$$\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}{=}\text{CHCH}_2\text{CH}_3 + \text{H}_2\text{O} \xrightarrow{\text{dil. H}_2\text{SO}_4\ \text{catalyst}} \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH(OH)CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$$
(All C–H bonds are drawn out in the full structural formulae.)

questions.question:
A student performs an experiment to determine the concentration of a solution of hypochlorous acid, HOCl ($K_a = 3.5 \times 10^{-8}$). The student starts with 25.00 mL of the acid in a conical flask and titrates it against a standardised solution of sodium hydroxide with a concentration of 1.47 mol L$^{-1}$. The equivalence point is reached after addition of 34.23 mL of NaOH.
$$\text{HOCl}(aq) + \text{OH}^-(aq) \rightarrow \text{OCl}^-(aq) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(l)$$

Calculate the concentration of the HOCl.
questions.answer:
At the equivalence point, $n(\text{HOCl}) = n(\text{NaOH})$ (1 : 1 ratio).

$n(\text{NaOH}) = 1.47 \times 0.03423 = 0.05032$ mol
$$c(\text{HOCl}) = \frac{0.05032}{0.02500} = 2.01\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$$

questions.question:
A student performs an experiment to determine the concentration of a solution of hypochlorous acid, HOCl ($K_a = 3.5 \times 10^{-8}$). The student starts with 25.00 mL of the acid in a conical flask and titrates it against a standardised solution of sodium hydroxide with a concentration of 1.47 mol L$^{-1}$. The equivalence point is reached after addition of 34.23 mL of NaOH.
$$\text{HOCl}(aq) + \text{OH}^-(aq) \rightarrow \text{OCl}^-(aq) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(l)$$

The concentration of the HOCl was found to be 2.01 mol L$^{-1}$. Determine the pH of the solution in the conical flask after the addition of 28.55 mL of NaOH.
questions.answer:
**Reaction (moles):**
- $n(\text{OH}^-) = 1.47 \times 0.02855 = 0.04197$ mol
- $n(\text{HOCl})_{\text{initial}} = 1.47 \times 0.03423 = 0.05032$ mol

| | HOCl | $\text{OH}^-$ | $\text{OCl}^-$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| Initial | 0.05032 | 0.04197 | 0 |
| Change | $-0.04197$ | $-0.04197$ | $+0.04197$ |
| End | 0.00835 | 0 | 0.04197 |

**Concentrations** (total volume $= 25.00 + 28.55 = 53.55$ mL):
- $[\text{HOCl}] = \dfrac{0.00835}{0.05355} = 0.1559$ mol L$^{-1}$
- $[\text{OCl}^-] = \dfrac{0.04197}{0.05355} = 0.7837$ mol L$^{-1}$

**Equilibrium:** $\text{HOCl} \rightleftharpoons \text{H}^+ + \text{OCl}^-$. Because $K_a$ is very small, the change $x$ is negligible:
$$K_a = \frac{[\text{H}^+][\text{OCl}^-]}{[\text{HOCl}]} \Rightarrow 3.5 \times 10^{-8} = \frac{x(0.7837)}{0.1559}$$
$$[\text{H}^+] = x = 6.96 \times 10^{-9}\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$$
$$\text{pH} = -\log_{10}(6.96 \times 10^{-9}) = 8.16$$

(Equivalently, for this buffer: $\text{pH} = \text{p}K_a + \log_{10}\dfrac{[\text{OCl}^-]}{[\text{HOCl}]} = 7.46 + 0.70 = 8.16$.)

questions.question:
A student performs an experiment to determine the concentration of a solution of hypochlorous acid, HOCl ($K_a = 3.5 \times 10^{-8}$). The student starts with 25.00 mL of the acid in a conical flask and titrates it against a standardised solution of sodium hydroxide with a concentration of 1.47 mol L$^{-1}$. The equivalence point is reached after addition of 34.23 mL of NaOH.
$$\text{HOCl}(aq) + \text{OH}^-(aq) \rightarrow \text{OCl}^-(aq) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(l)$$

From these results the student calculated the concentration of HOCl to be 2.01 mol L$^{-1}$. The actual concentration of the HOCl is found to be 1.85 mol L$^{-1}$. Qualitatively discuss whether the following error may have contributed to the student's results: *The student rinsed the burette with distilled water instead of NaOH solution before filling it with NaOH.*
questions.answer:
Rinsing with distilled water leaves water in the burette, which dilutes the NaOH to below 1.47 mol L$^{-1}$. More of the diluted NaOH is needed to reach the equivalence point, so the titre (34.23 mL) is larger than it should be. In the calculation the student still uses 1.47 mol L$^{-1}$ multiplied by this larger volume. That overestimates the moles of NaOH, and so the moles and concentration of HOCl.

So this error makes the calculated concentration too high, and it could have contributed to the student's result: 2.01 mol L$^{-1}$ is higher than the actual 1.85 mol L$^{-1}$.

To check the size: the actual $n(\text{HOCl}) = 1.85 \times 0.02500 = 0.0463$ mol, which needs only 31.5 mL of 1.47 mol L$^{-1}$ NaOH. A 34.23 mL titre means the NaOH was really about 1.35 mol L$^{-1}$, roughly 8% diluted. Leftover rinse water could plausibly cause that.

*Note: the paper's marking guideline was written for a version with an actual concentration of 2.25 mol L$^{-1}$ and concludes that the error could not explain the result. With the value 1.85 mol L$^{-1}$ printed in the exam, the conclusion is reversed.*

questions.question:
A halogenated organic compound M with a molar mass of 94.54 g mol$^{-1}$ is known to produce TWO products, compounds N and O, when heated with concentrated $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$:
$$\text{M} \xrightarrow{\text{conc. H}_2\text{SO}_4} \text{N} + \text{O}$$
A chemist obtained the infrared and mass spectra for compound M (first image), and the proton and carbon-13 NMR spectra for products N and O (second image). Proton NMR data are given in the table (third image).

Draw the structure and name each of the compounds M, N and O. Justify your answer with reference to all the information provided.
questions.answer:
**Compound M: 1-chloropropan-2-ol**, $\text{ClCH}_2\text{–CH(OH)–CH}_3$

- **IR:** the very broad, strong absorption centred near 3400 cm$^{-1}$ is an O–H stretch, which shows an alcohol. There is no strong C=O absorption near 1700 cm$^{-1}$.
- **Molecular ion:** the mass spectrum has a small molecular ion peak at $m/z = 94$ and a peak at 96 in about a 3 : 1 ratio. This is the pattern of the $^{35}\text{Cl}$/$^{37}\text{Cl}$ isotopes, so M has one Cl atom. $\text{C}_3\text{H}_7\text{ClO}$ has $M = 3(12.01) + 7(1.008) + 35.45 + 16.00 = 94.54$ g mol$^{-1}$, which matches.
- **Fragments:**

| $m/z$ | Fragment | Information |
|---|---|---|
| 79/81 | $[\text{M} - \text{CH}_3]^+$ | contains Cl |
| 49/51 (base peak) | $[\text{CH}_2\text{Cl}]^+$ | Cl is on a terminal $\text{CH}_2$ |
| 45 | $[\text{CH}_3\text{CHOH}]^+$ | no Cl; OH on the middle carbon next to the $\text{CH}_3$ |
| 15 | $[\text{CH}_3]^+$ | methyl group |

- **Reaction:** concentrated sulfuric acid dehydrates alcohols. Removing the –OH from C2 with an H from either neighbouring carbon gives two different alkenes, $\text{C}_3\text{H}_5\text{Cl}$. This explains why there are two products.

**Compound N: 1-chloroprop-1-ene**, $\text{ClCH{=}CH–CH}_3$ (H removed from the $\text{CH}_2\text{Cl}$ carbon)

- **$^{13}$C NMR:** 3 signals. The signals at about 130 and 105 ppm are the two sp$^2$ carbons of a C=C. The signal at about 15 ppm is an alkyl $\text{CH}_3$ that is not attached to Cl.
- **$^1$H NMR:**

| Shift (ppm) | Integration | Splitting | Assignment |
|---|---|---|---|
| ~1.8 | 3H | doublet | $\text{CH}_3$ next to one H |
| ~5.7 | 1H | doublet | alkene =CHCl, next to one H |
| ~6.0 | 1H | multiplet | alkene =CH–, coupled to both the =CHCl and the $\text{CH}_3$ |

This gives the chain Cl–CH=CH–CH$_3$.

**Compound O: 3-chloroprop-1-ene**, $\text{CH}_2{=}\text{CH–CH}_2\text{Cl}$ (H removed from the $\text{CH}_3$ carbon)

- **$^{13}$C NMR:** 3 signals. The signals at about 135 and 118 ppm are the C=C carbons. The signal at about 45 ppm is an sp$^3$ carbon shifted downfield by the electronegative Cl, which shows a $\text{CH}_2\text{Cl}$ group.
- **$^1$H NMR:**

| Shift (ppm) | Integration | Splitting | Assignment |
|---|---|---|---|
| ~4.0 | 2H | doublet | $\text{CH}_2\text{Cl}$ next to one H |
| ~5.0 | 2H | doublet | =$\text{CH}_2$ |
| ~6.2 | 1H | multiplet | =CH–, between the two $\text{CH}_2$ groups |

This gives the chain $\text{CH}_2$=CH–$\text{CH}_2$Cl.

questions.question:
A commercial disinfectant is reported to have two active ingredients, hydrogen peroxide ($\text{H}_2\text{O}_2$) and peracetic acid ($\text{CH}_3\text{COOOH}$), at concentrations of 4% and 12% (w/v) respectively. A titration experiment was carried out to confirm the accuracy of these values.

A 10.00 mL sample of the disinfectant solution was transferred to a 100 mL volumetric flask, which was filled to the mark with demineralised water. 20.00 mL of the resultant solution was transferred to a conical flask containing 5.000 mL of 3.000 mol L$^{-1}$ sulfuric acid and titrated with a 0.2491 mol L$^{-1}$ cerium sulfate solution.

Equation 1: $\text{H}_2\text{O}_2(aq) + 2\text{Ce(SO}_4)_2(aq) \rightarrow \text{Ce}_2(\text{SO}_4)_3(aq) + \text{H}_2\text{SO}_4(aq) + \text{O}_2(g)$

| Titre | Volume of $\text{Ce(SO}_4)_2$ added (mL) |
|---|---|
| 1 | 21.65 |
| 2 | 21.15 |
| 3 | 21.20 |
| 4 | 21.30 |

Immediately after, 5.000 mL of a 20% (w/v) potassium iodide solution was added to the conical flask containing titre 4. This reacts with the sulfuric acid to produce hydroiodic acid, which then reduces the peracetic acid present in the sample and forms iodine.

Equation 2: $2\text{KI}(aq) + \text{H}_2\text{SO}_4(aq) \rightarrow 2\text{HI}(aq) + \text{K}_2\text{SO}_4(aq)$

Equation 3: $\text{CH}_3\text{COOOH}(aq) + 2\text{HI}(aq) \rightarrow \text{I}_2(aq) + \text{CH}_3\text{COOH}(aq) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(l)$

The resultant iodine solution was titrated with a 0.2250 mol L$^{-1}$ solution of sodium thiosulfate, and a titre volume of 27.35 mL was required to reach the end point.

Equation 4: $\text{I}_2(aq) + 2\text{Na}_2\text{S}_2\text{O}_3(aq) \rightarrow \text{Na}_2\text{S}_4\text{O}_6(aq) + 2\text{NaI}(aq)$

Do the results of this experiment support the reported concentration values? Support your answer with calculations.
questions.answer:
**Hydrogen peroxide**

Titre 1 is an outlier (rough titre), so average titres 2–4:
$$V_{\text{avg}} = \frac{21.15 + 21.20 + 21.30}{3} = 21.22\ \text{mL}$$

$n(\text{Ce}^{4+}) = 0.2491 \times 0.02122 = 5.286 \times 10^{-3}$ mol

$n(\text{H}_2\text{O}_2) = \tfrac12 \times 5.286 \times 10^{-3} = 2.643 \times 10^{-3}$ mol in 20.00 mL of diluted solution

Scale up through the dilution:
- In 100 mL of diluted solution (= 10.00 mL of disinfectant): $2.643 \times 10^{-3} \times 5 = 1.321 \times 10^{-2}$ mol
- In 100 mL of original disinfectant: $1.321 \times 10^{-2} \times 10 = 0.1321$ mol

$m(\text{H}_2\text{O}_2) = 0.1321 \times 34.016 = 4.49$ g per 100 mL, i.e. **4.5% (w/v)**

**Peracetic acid**

$n(\text{S}_2\text{O}_3^{2-}) = 0.2250 \times 0.02735 = 6.154 \times 10^{-3}$ mol

$n(\text{I}_2) = \tfrac12 \times 6.154 \times 10^{-3} = 3.077 \times 10^{-3}$ mol, so $n(\text{CH}_3\text{COOOH}) = 3.077 \times 10^{-3}$ mol in 20.00 mL

In 100 mL of original disinfectant: $3.077 \times 10^{-3} \times 5 \times 10 = 0.1538$ mol

$m(\text{CH}_3\text{COOOH}) = 0.1538 \times 76.05 = 11.70$ g per 100 mL, i.e. **11.7% (w/v)**

**Evaluation**

The measured peracetic acid concentration (11.7%) is within about 2.5% of the reported 12%, so the results support the stated peracetic acid content. The measured hydrogen peroxide concentration (4.5%) is about 12% higher than the reported 4%. So the results do not closely support the stated hydrogen peroxide value; the disinfectant contains somewhat more $\text{H}_2\text{O}_2$ than reported.

*Note: the paper's sample answer gets the same values (4.494% and 11.70%) but concludes the opposite, that the $\text{H}_2\text{O}_2$ value is accurate and the peracetic acid value is not. The percentage differences show the reverse is true.*
